transcript: As of August 2nd, yesterday, your AI product just became illegal. And you don't have any idea why, but governments just flipped the switch. The EU AI Act went live this week. New transparency obligations are enforceable right now. And they all revolve around one term you've never heard of. S-G-I. Synthetically Generated Information. term you've never heard of, SGI, synthetically generated information. So if your product uses an AI model to write any copy, generate images, create avatars, or produce any content that your users are consuming, you are now distributing SGI. And if you do not disclose that to your users, you are now legally liable for deceptive practices in every jurisdiction that has adopted these new rules. So, your AI never told you this existed because it didn't know. But here are the three things you direct your AI to build before a regulator catches you. Step one, explicit labeling on every AI-generated output your product produces.labeling on every AI-generated output your product produces. Not a footnote, not a buried disclaimer, but a very visible, non-removable disclosure that tells the user this content was generated by AI. The regulations are very specific. Watermarks on synthetic media, disclaimers on generated text, metadata tags on AI-produced images, and your AI can build this labeling system in one day. So that's a win. Step 2. Hard consent before any user input touches an AI model. If your app takes a user's photo and runs it through a model, or takes their text and rewrites it in AI, the user has to opt in explicitly. Not a pre-checked box, not a buried clause in your Terms of Service. An affirmative action by the user before their data enters the model. So direct your AI to build a consent gate on every feature that processes user input through AI. And step 3, a generation log that proves what your system produced and when. If a government audit asks what your AI generated last Tuesday, you have to have an answer. A secure, immutable log of every AI output with a timestamp, the model used, and the input that triggered it. Direct your AI to instrument this on every generation endpoint. The builders who have this log demonstrate compliance. The builders who do not have it demonstrate negligence. So the rules have changed this week for everyone. And your AI does not read legislation. That's your job. So direct your AI to comply before someone directs you to shut it down. That's a win.

claims.topic: EU AI Act transparency obligations for AI-generated content and AI-processed user input
claims.problem: The speaker claims that, as of August 2, new EU AI Act transparency obligations are enforceable and make AI products legally exposed if they generate user-consumed content or process user input through AI without visible disclosure, explicit consent, and auditable generation records.
technicalClaims: The speaker claims that any product using an AI model to write copy, generate images, create avatars, or otherwise produce content consumed by users is distributing “Synthetically Generated Information” (SGI). In the speaker’s framing, undisclosed SGI creates legal liability for deceptive practices in every jurisdiction that has adopted the new rules.

The speaker claims that every AI-generated output must carry explicit labeling: a very visible, non-removable disclosure stating that the content was generated by AI. They distinguish this from insufficient approaches such as footnotes or buried disclaimers, and cite watermarks for synthetic media, disclaimers for generated text, and metadata tags for AI-produced images as required or expected mechanisms.

The speaker claims that user input must not be sent to an AI model unless the user has first provided hard, explicit consent. They give examples such as a user photo being run through a model or user text being rewritten by AI, and specify that consent must be an affirmative action rather than a pre-checked box or a clause buried in Terms of Service.

The speaker claims that each AI generation endpoint needs a secure, immutable generation log recording every AI output, the timestamp, the model used, and the input that triggered the output. They claim this log is needed to answer government audit questions about what the system generated at a particular time, and that having the log demonstrates compliance while lacking it demonstrates negligence.
claims.recommendedSolution: Treat the speaker’s proposed compliance work as a hypothesis to test against the actual product and applicable law: add explicit visible/non-removable AI-generated-content labeling to every AI output; add affirmative consent gates before any feature sends user input to an AI model; and instrument every generation endpoint with a secure, immutable audit log containing output, timestamp, model identity, and triggering input. The speaker further claims an AI coding assistant can build the labeling system in one day, but this implementation-effort estimate should be validated rather than assumed.
reasoning: The alleged regulatory mechanism is that enforceable transparency obligations now apply to SGI; if an application distributes AI-generated content without disclosure, the user may be deceived and the builder may become legally liable. Visible labeling is claimed to change that mechanism by making the AI origin of each output explicit to users.

For generated media and text, the speaker’s proposed implementation mechanisms are output-type-specific disclosures: watermarks for synthetic media, visible disclaimers for generated text, and metadata tags for AI-produced images. The claimed outcome is that users can recognize AI-generated material at the point of consumption rather than relying on hidden or indirect notices.

For user inputs, the alleged risk mechanism is that user data can enter an AI model without meaningful user permission. A consent gate before AI processing is claimed to prevent that by requiring an affirmative opt-in before the model receives photos, text, or other user-provided data.

For audits, the alleged risk mechanism is lack of evidence: if regulators ask what the AI generated on a specific date, the system cannot prove its behavior without records. Logging every generation with timestamp, model, triggering input, and output is claimed to create an audit trail that can demonstrate compliance.

The speaker presents the rules as broadly applicable to “everyone” building AI products, but the technical applicability still depends on whether the repository actually contains AI generation or AI-processing features and whether those features are in jurisdictions covered by the cited obligations.
assumptions: The product contains AI features that generate content consumed by users, process user input through an AI model, or both.
The product is offered in, or otherwise subject to, jurisdictions where the cited EU AI Act transparency obligations or similar adopted rules apply.
The term “Synthetically Generated Information” and the specific disclosure, consent, and logging duties are legally applicable to the product as the speaker describes.
All AI-generated outputs and all AI-processing entry points can be identified in the codebase, including indirect generation paths, background jobs, third-party AI integrations, and API endpoints.
The application has enough control over its UI, generated media, image metadata, and delivery channels to make disclosures visible and non-removable as the speaker recommends.

The system can persist the proposed audit data—inputs, outputs, model used, and timestamps—in a secure and immutable form without violating other privacy, data-minimization, retention, or user-deletion obligations; the speaker does not address those tradeoffs.

A repository implementation alone is sufficient to enforce labels, consent gates, and logging across deployed environments; in practice this may also depend on configuration, infrastructure, third-party services, and operational controls.

implications.detail: The speaker recommends a secure, immutable log of generation activity, implying controls against tampering with audit evidence.
If generation logging is incomplete or absent, the speaker claims the system may be unable to answer regulator questions about what was generated and when.
AI generation and AI-processing paths would need consistent cross-cutting enforcement points for labeling, consent collection, and audit logging across all relevant endpoints and output surfaces.
Future AI features would need to be added in a way that preserves the labeling, consent, and logging behavior, or they could bypass the claimed compliance controls.
Compliance depends not only on code paths existing but on deployed logging, retention, and audit-retrieval processes being operational when a government audit occurs.

The speaker frames the work as something to direct an AI coding assistant to implement, but the repository audit should verify the generated changes rather than assuming the assistant understands current legislation or product-specific obligations.

uncertainties: The transcript makes legal claims about the EU AI Act, SGI, enforceability as of August 2, and liability for deceptive practices; a repository audit cannot validate those legal interpretations without legal review.

Repository inspection can identify whether AI generation/processing integrations exist, whether outputs are labeled in UI/media/metadata code, whether consent gates are implemented before model calls, and whether generation endpoints are instrumented for logging.
Repository inspection may not prove that disclosures are actually visible to users in all deployed clients, locales, A/B tests, or rendering contexts; runtime UI review may be needed.
Repository inspection may not prove that labels are truly non-removable once content is exported, screenshotted, downloaded, transformed, or shared through third-party platforms.

Repository inspection can check for logging code and schema fields, but production evidence is needed to confirm that logs are complete, immutable, retained, queryable, protected from tampering, and available for the time period regulators might ask about.

The speaker’s proposed logging of user inputs and AI outputs may create privacy, security, retention, or data-minimization issues not discussed in the transcript; whether that design is acceptable depends on product context and applicable law.

The transcript does not specify which model types, third-party providers, user roles, jurisdictions, exemptions, or risk classifications are in scope, so applicability must be established separately before treating the recommendation as mandatory.

onboardingPrompt:
You are performing a read-only repository onboarding for a follow-up audit about AI-generated content and AI-processed user input transparency. Do not edit files, implement changes, create commits, or recommend a solution yet. Your job is to understand how this repository currently works so a later prompt can test specific compliance-related hypotheses against evidence. Do not assume a legal problem exists, and do not make legal conclusions.

Focus only on repository and configuration evidence. Separate confirmed facts from inference and unknowns. Cite exact file paths and precise symbols: routes, controllers, API clients, UI components, schemas, migrations, feature flags, settings, tests, background jobs, event names, dashboards-as-code, and docs. If runtime or production evidence is needed, state that explicitly rather than guessing.

Map the current system in these areas:

1. Repository shape and runtime boundaries
- Identify applications/packages/services, frontend clients, backend APIs, workers, shared libraries, infrastructure-as-code, and relevant deployment/config directories.
- Note frameworks, languages, data stores, queue/event systems, object storage/CDN/media pipelines, authentication/authorization, analytics/observability stacks, and environment/configuration mechanisms.
- Identify owners or CODEOWNERS if present.

2. AI/model integration inventory
- Search for direct and indirect AI/model usage: provider SDKs, HTTP clients, internal ML services, prompt templates, generation utilities, embeddings/classification/rewrite/image/avatar/media functions, third-party integrations, background tasks, and feature flags.
- For each integration, record provider/service, model/config source if visible, call sites, request and response shapes, whether user input appears to be included, whether output is consumed by users or only internal systems, and whether calls happen synchronously, asynchronously, or offline.
- Include evidence for absence where meaningful, but avoid overclaiming if repository layout or dynamic configuration limits certainty.

3. User input and output surface flows
- Trace materially relevant flows from user-facing entry points to downstream processing: text forms/editors, uploads, photos/images, profile/avatar features, chat/messages, content creation tools, moderation/rewrite/summarization, and APIs that accept user-provided content.
- Trace outputs from AI/model call sites to rendering or delivery surfaces: web/mobile UI components, generated text blocks, images/media files, metadata, emails/notifications, downloadable/exported assets, shared/public pages, API responses, and stored records.
- Capture routing boundaries and transformations where labels, notices, metadata, media processing, storage, or sharing behavior could be applied or lost. Do not judge sufficiency yet.

4. Existing user-facing controls, notices, and preferences
- Inventory current UI patterns and backend records related to user permissions, opt-ins, privacy settings, consent/acknowledgment modals, disclosure banners/badges, content provenance indicators, and terms/privacy policy references.
- Record whether these appear globally reusable or feature-specific, and how state is persisted and checked before sensitive processing. Report only what the repository shows.

5. Persistence, auditability, logging, and observability
- Identify schemas/tables/collections/events/log records associated with AI/model calls, generated content, user input processing, content history, consent/preferences, audit logs, security logs, telemetry, and analytics.
- Record available fields, retention/configuration hints, access controls, immutability/append-only mechanisms if any, redaction/encryption patterns, correlation IDs, and model/version capture if present.
- Distinguish application logs, analytics events, database records, object storage metadata, and external observability integrations.

6. Tests and verification assets
- Inventory tests that exercise AI/model calls, generated output display, upload/media processing, consent/preference flows, logging/audit events, and configuration variants. Include unit, integration, e2e, contract, snapshot, and policy tests.
- Note mocks/stubs that may obscure production behavior.

Deliver a concise architecture briefing with:
- System overview and relevant runtime boundaries.
- AI/model integration table: file path/symbol, trigger, input source, output destination, provider/model config, sync/async, known tests.
- User input to processing flow map and generated output delivery flow map.
- Existing controls/notices/preferences and logging/audit/persistence inventory.
- Configuration and deployment factors that may change behavior by environment, tenant, role, locale, or jurisdiction.
- Confirmed facts vs inferences vs unknowns needing runtime or legal/business input.
- A short handoff map for the follow-up audit: highest-value files/symbols/routes/schemas/tests to inspect first, and what cannot be determined statically.

Stop after the briefing and wait for the next prompt. Do not propose or implement changes.
investigationPrompt:
You are performing a read-only repository investigation of a compliance-oriented hypothesis about AI-generated content and AI-processed user input. Do not edit files, implement changes, create commits, or refactor. Use the onboarding briefing if available, but independently verify important evidence.

Hypothesis to test, not assume: subject to legal review and actual product scope, the product may need explicit visible/non-removable AI-origin labeling for user-consumed AI-generated outputs; affirmative user consent before user input is sent to an AI model; and secure, immutable generation audit records containing output, timestamp, model identity/version, and triggering input. The source also claims these obligations are enforceable under EU AI Act-style transparency rules as of August 2, uses the term “Synthetically Generated Information” for AI-produced content, and estimates that an AI coding assistant could build labeling in one day. Treat the legal interpretation, terminology, jurisdictional reach, and effort estimate as uncertain. Repository inspection can establish technical facts; it cannot validate legal applicability or production operation without legal, product, runtime, and deployment evidence.

Your output must be evidence-backed and claim-specific. For every material claim below, assign one applicability status: Confirmed, Partially Applicable, Refuted, Not Applicable, or Needs Runtime Verification. Include exact static repository evidence, missing evidence, assumptions, realistic impact, severity where meaningful, and confidence. If static evidence is mixed and runtime proof is missing, preserve both facts rather than collapsing to a stronger conclusion.

Severity guidance: use Critical, High, Medium, Low, or Informational only when tied to actual exposure, frequency, user scale, jurisdictional reach, exploitability/tamperability, reliability of failure, and operational cost. Do not exaggerate a theoretical concern into a production issue. If legal applicability is unresolved, say so and temper severity accordingly.

Investigation methodology

1. Establish technical and jurisdictional scope gates
- Determine whether the repository contains AI/model features that generate content consumed by users, process user-provided input, or both. Include direct provider calls, internal ML services, background jobs, batch generation, third-party tools, plugins, feature flags, and generated media pipelines.
- Identify output types: text, copy, recommendations, summaries, images, avatars, audio/video, metadata, API payloads, emails, public/shared pages, downloads/exports, and admin-only/internal outputs.
- Identify deployment or configuration hints relevant to EU or other jurisdictional exposure: region flags, tenant config, locales, geo restrictions, product editions, environment variables, or docs. Do not infer legal applicability from code alone.
- If no AI/model processing exists, most downstream claims may be Not Applicable, but document search methods and evidence.

2. Test the “AI-generated user-consumed content / SGI” claim technically
- Build an inventory of generation entry points and trace each from trigger to model call to storage/transformation to consumption surface.
- For each path, record whether generated content is actually user-consumed, internal-only, admin-only, or ambiguous. Note public distribution vs private display vs ephemeral response.
- Evidence to cite: routes/controllers, service methods, prompt builders, provider clients, queues/jobs, schemas, UI components, serialization/API response code, object storage/media code, and tests.
- Static limits: repository inspection can show likely flows and code paths, but not production traffic frequency, enabled flags, tenant adoption, or actual jurisdictions served without deployment/analytics evidence.

3. Test visible AI-origin labeling and output provenance mechanisms
- For every user-consumed AI output path, inspect where the output is rendered or delivered. Look for existing visible indicators, badges, labels, disclaimers, content provenance fields, media overlays/watermarks, image metadata tags, API provenance fields, email text, or public-page notices.
- Distinguish output-type mechanisms: generated text disclosures, synthetic media watermarking/overlays, image metadata tags, avatar/image generation provenance, downloadable/exported asset handling, and downstream transformations that may strip or omit provenance.
- Evaluate static evidence of visibility and persistence: is a notice coupled to the output component or optional/conditional? Is it server-rendered or client-only? Is it hidden behind a tooltip, footnote, settings panel, or terms link? Does export/share/download code include or drop provenance? Do image/media optimization steps preserve metadata or overlays?
- Do not declare labels “visible” or “non-removable” solely from code if actual rendering, CSS, responsive layouts, locales, A/B tests, or third-party platform behavior are unverified. Mark those aspects Needs Runtime Verification and identify specific UI review or artifact inspection needed.
- Consider counterevidence: output clearly not generated by AI, output internal-only, generation disabled by config, or labels already present at the exact consumption point.

4. Test affirmative consent before AI processing of user input
- Inventory all user input sources that may reach AI/model calls: text editors, prompts, messages, uploaded photos/images, files, profile data, support tickets, documents, voice/video, and API-supplied content.
- Trace each source to the model call. Identify where any consent, opt-in, privacy preference, acknowledgment, or feature enablement is collected; how it is represented in state; where it is enforced before the model receives input; and how it is tested.
- Assess whether the repository shows an affirmative action rather than default-on behavior, pre-checked boxes, implied acceptance via terms, or post-processing notice. Evidence may include UI components, form defaults, backend validators/guards, database consent records, API middleware, and tests.
- Note whether consent is scoped to a feature/data type/model provider, tenant, user role, locale, or time; whether revocation exists; and whether backend enforcement prevents bypassing UI-only consent.
- Static limits: code can show intended gates and defaults, but not whether production UI displays as expected, whether historical users consented, whether consent records are complete, or whether all third-party integrations behave as configured.

5. Test generation audit logging, integrity, and retrievability
- Inventory every generation/model-processing endpoint or job and identify logging/persistence at or near the call site. For each path, check whether records include timestamp, model/provider identity or version, triggering input or reference, generated output or reference, user/tenant/request correlation, feature name, and status/error fields.
- Distinguish application logs, analytics events, audit tables, content history tables, prompt/response stores, object storage metadata, vendor logs, and observability traces. Do not treat debug logs as immutable audit records unless evidence supports it.
- Evaluate static evidence of security and immutability: append-only tables, migrations, restricted update/delete paths, WORM/object-lock storage, signed/hash-chained records, write-once event streams, IAM policies, database permissions, encryption/redaction, audit access controls, and retention/deletion configuration.
- Assess operational retrievability: are there query paths, admin tools, exports, dashboards, documented procedures, or schemas that would let the team answer “what did the system generate at a particular time?” Identify whether production evidence is required to confirm completeness, retention, tamper resistance, and access.
- Analyze tradeoffs and constraints: storing full user inputs and outputs can conflict with privacy, data minimization, sensitive-data handling, retention limits, user deletion rights, and security risk. Do not recommend blanket full-payload logging unless these constraints are addressed.

6. Assess mitigations, counterevidence, and solution fit
- Current mitigations: identify existing labels/provenance, consent/preference infrastructure, AI gateway abstractions, centralized model clients, policy middleware, audit/event pipelines, media processing hooks, privacy controls, and tests that reduce risk or provide reusable enforcement points.
- Bypass risks: direct provider calls outside a central gateway, background jobs, admin tools, imports, retry paths, cached/generated content reuse, exported/downloaded media, API clients, feature flags, tenant-specific code, localization, and third-party-hosted generation.
- Causal chain: for each claim, state whether the repository supports the alleged chain from AI use → user exposure or input processing → missing/weak transparency/permission/evidence → realistic compliance/operational risk. Break the chain where evidence is absent.
- Side effects and operational cost: assess storage volume and sensitivity, latency, UX friction, media-processing complexity, metadata stripping by CDNs, migration of existing content, audit access processes, incident response, monitoring, and maintenance for future AI features.
- Smaller or safer alternatives to consider if the broad recommendation overfits: centralizing model calls before adding feature-specific controls, labeling only confirmed user-consumed generated outputs, storing references/hashes/redacted prompts instead of raw payloads where appropriate, server-side enforcement of consent on high-risk flows, or gathering legal/runtime evidence before broad logging. Do not implement.
- Validate the one-day labeling estimate against repository reality: number of surfaces, clients, output types, localization, design system availability, export/media handling, tests required, and release/deployment complexity. Treat as an estimate assessment, not a task plan.

Required report format

A. Executive summary
- Overall recommendation disposition: Proceed, Modify Recommendation, Reject, or Gather More Evidence.
- One-paragraph rationale grounded in repository evidence and uncertainty.

B. Applicability matrix
Create a compact table with rows for at least:
1) AI-generated user-consumed content exists.
2) AI-processed user input exists.
3) Jurisdiction/legal applicability can be established from repo/config.
4) Visible labeling/provenance exists for generated text.
5) Watermark/overlay/provenance exists for synthetic media or avatars, if applicable.
6) Metadata tags/provenance exist for AI-produced images, if applicable.
7) Affirmative consent is collected before model processing of user input.
8) Backend enforcement prevents consent bypass.
9) Generation audit records include timestamp, model identity/version, triggering input, and output/reference.
10) Audit records appear secure, immutable, retained, and retrievable.
11) The proposed implementation effort estimate is plausible.

Columns: Claim, Status, Severity, Static evidence with exact paths/symbols, Missing/runtime evidence, Assumptions, Realistic impact, Confidence.

C. Evidence details
- Provide source-to-sink traces for representative and high-risk AI paths. Include exact files/symbols and summarize data/control flow.
- Include current tests and gaps. Do not run destructive tests. If you run safe read-only tests/searches, say what you ran and results.

D. Static vs runtime/legal boundary
- Explicitly list what static inspection established.
- Explicitly list what needs runtime evidence: traces, logs, query results, production configuration, feature-flag state, traffic/user scale, UI screenshots/artifact inspection, media downloads, EXIF/metadata checks, retention settings, IAM/policy verification, and audit retrieval drills.
- Explicitly list what needs legal/product review: EU AI Act interpretation, “SGI” terminology, enforceability date, jurisdictional scope, exemptions, risk classification, consent requirements, and privacy/data-minimization tradeoffs.

E. Recommendation fit
- State whether to Proceed, Modify Recommendation, Reject, or Gather More Evidence.
- Identify any parts that should remain untouched for now, especially areas where repository evidence shows no AI use, internal-only flows, legal scope uncertainty, or privacy risk from over-logging.
- Provide open questions for legal, product, design, security, privacy, and operations.

End with an explicit STOP. Do not include implementation code, patches, commits, or refactors.
